source.title: Grokking revisited: reverse engineering grokking modulo addition in LSTM

record.file_problem: The post text is present, but several referenced figures and diagrams are not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests grokking on modular addition using an LSTM, a different architecture from the original transformer setting.
record.gate_note: The post explicitly reports observing grokking, but gives no numerical training/test-accuracy trajectory or training-set-size sweep in the supplied text. Several figure references have no accompanying extracted values. Weight-decay and Adam beta settings are described as choices informed by prior work/grid search, not results.
record.test_reason: The post trains an LSTM on a+b mod 113 with 30% of pairs and reports grokking, a new architecture for the original algorithmic setting. It also gives a qualitative account of how the embedding periodicity develops during training. No accuracy numbers or dataset-size sweep appear in the supplied text.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also claim to have fully reverse-engineered the algorithm, and that a much simpler equivalent model groks too.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modulo addition and training choices similar to the cited grokking work, but applies them to an LSTM with ReLU cell-to-hidden activation, hidden dimension 113, one-hot inputs, and a two-matrix linear output factorization.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports that a simplified model groks with the output linear map factorized into two matrices but not with one matrix. Replacing selected gates or activations in the original model is reported not to change accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing or replacing gates and activations preserves accuracy. The extracted simplified model is about 5% less accurate than the original.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The LSTM's grokked solution uses only a small part of the LSTM's capacity and reduces to two embedding lookups, a ReLU, and a matrix.

fits_no_version.finding: The learned algorithm learns 113 sum-specific constants and relies on sums of roots of unity being small. Sums omitted from training are more often wrong.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An LSTM's grokked modular-addition algorithm is partly empirical, unlike a fully general Fourier algorithm. This bears loosely on V6 (algorithm varies with architecture), but the post makes no explicit comparison.

record.problems: The supplied text gives no numerical train/test accuracy curve, no quantified timing of the test improvement, and no dataset-size comparison. Several figure references lack extracted figure contents; uncertainty estimates and controls are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: No separate row for the stated average peak Fourier magnitude over training: the referenced plot is not present and the text gives no extractable value or explicit numerical description. Hyperparameter choices and cited descriptions of prior work are excluded.

untested.parts: Chance-to-near-perfect accuracy values, quantified delay after train saturation, and dependence of the delay on training-set size.
Removal of memorizing components, and continuous progress measures shown to anticipate the test jump.
All parts. Weight decay is used but not varied.
No multi-run or explicit cross-architecture algorithm comparison.

missing.locator: Figure after 'observe grokking' (Model architecture section), not in text

missing.what: Average peak Fourier magnitude over the training run (a progress-like measure)
missing.locator: Reverse engineering simplified model, missing figure

missing.what: Authors state the two-linear-layer trick 'makes grokking easier' for the full LSTM. This is a method dependence with no row.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong post with no numbers in the text, and all evidence is qualitative. The hyperparameters follow Nanda (large weight decay, grid-searched Adam betas) and were not varied, so V5 and V7 are untested. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The post reports grokking on one 30% training split, but does not provide the chance-to-near-perfect accuracy values, quantify the delay after training accuracy saturates, or compare delay across training-set sizes.

It reports periodic embeddings emerging early and later frequency diversification, but does not show memorizing components being removed later or demonstrate that a continuous progress measure predicts the test-accuracy jump.
No non-algorithmic dataset, initialization-scale sweep, or weight-norm/lazy-to-rich comparison.
No LLM pretraining or realistic-data fine-tuning.
Weight decay is used, but its efficiency account, critical dataset size, and ungrokking prediction are not tested.
The post does not compare algorithms learned across multiple runs or architectures/hyperparameters.
No adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifact controls are tested.

conditions.value: 30% of all pairs; reshuffled training data omitting a particular sum

rows.measure: Learned representation / errors on sums missing from the training data
rows.value: The model learns 113 values of c′ separately rather than 113²; when the training data is reshuffled to omit a particular sum, it is more likely to get that sum wrong.
rows.note: This describes the learned algorithm and a training-data dependency, not a comparison of grokking delays across dataset sizes.
rows.check: This describes the learned algorithm and a sensitivity to omitted sums. It bears on no version, and 'partial' is not meaningful here.
